explanations.text:
●  the page loads the project                           ([script](script))
│     The page asks for one record, human.json, that names the files
│     of the project. For every file it then asks for the record of
│     its abstractions, explanation_<name>.json in the map folder. A
│     file with no record gets an empty one, so the page still shows
│     it. The file itself comes only when you open the file. The
│     human.json is always in the list, first, under the name
│     human/human.json. It also asks for project.json, the record
│     about the project as a whole; when it holds abstractions it
│     joins the list too, under the name human/project.json. The
│     human.json also names the human files, the tellings with no
│     code under them; for each one the page asks for its record,
│     human_<name>.json, and it joins the list after project.json
│     and before the files, under the name human/human_<name>.json.
│     Every five seconds it [asks for human.json again](refreshFiles);
│     when the files or the human files in it changed, the tree shows
│     the new list, and the file you read stays open, or the first
│     file opens when yours is gone.
│
●  the page draws the file tree                             ([main](main))
│     On the left: the project name and its files. A click on a
│     file opens that file. Above the files, new file opens a box
│     for a name; enter [asks the server to make that file](makeNamed),
│     and escape, or a second click on new file, closes the box. The
│     server's answer shows on top of the reader: a pass opens the new
│     file and marks it in the tree, and a refusal stays in the
│     warning colour. Beside new file, new human file opens the same
│     box for a bare name, like payments, and makes a human file, a
│     telling with no code under it; a click on the other word turns
│     the box to that kind and empties it.
│
●  the page opens one file                                  ([open](open))
│     It keeps the lines of the file and every abstraction, and it
│     remembers which piece of the file each abstraction is about.
│     It also remembers which abstractions you left open, so a file
│     you come back to opens as you left it. A writing box left open
│     closes when you go to another file.
│
●  the page puts the abstractions in order               ([sorted](sorted))
│     A pin points from one abstraction at another. The abstraction
│     nobody points at is the most abstract, and it goes last. An
│     abstraction that a pin points at goes above the one that holds
│     the pin, and so on upward. Among equals, the one about earlier
│     lines goes first.
│
●  the page draws the list                              ([render](render))
│     Every abstraction is one header line: a small arrow, the name
│     of its piece and its lines. All start folded the first time.
│     Under the header the words are drawn exactly as written. A pin
│     whose target has an abstraction is lit; a pin with none is
│     muted; a pin the map does not hold yet, one you just typed, is
│     [read from the target it names](guessAnchor). The bar on top
│     says how many are open, the word unsaved while a change is only
│     in the page, and [a compile button](header) as soon as anything
│     differs from the map. A place for the words you expand on stands
│     on top of the list while the ask is open; a file with no map
│     shows one place for its telling and the code of the file under
│     it, and the bar says there is no abstraction yet, in the place of
│     the count, with the compiling mark beside it. Only human.json
│     takes no writing. A human file, and the project, show the
│     telling alone, because they have no code. An entry whose
│     writing waits for claude is marked compiling, with a count when
│     more than one waits. A redraw keeps the page where you had
│     scrolled it, so the words stay under your eyes. The head line of
│     an abstraction you asked to take away holds that ask in the
│     place of its name until you send it or drop it.
│
●  you write                                          ([the box](startEdit))
│     A click on the words puts a box in their place, with the caret
│     where you clicked. A muted pin shows a name beside its words,
│     and that name counts too, so a click after one lands where you
│     meant. It holds the text as it is in the map — the pins in
│     their brackets, the targets visible — or the code of the file,
│     or nothing for a new abstraction. The box grows as you type,
│     and the page stays where you scrolled it. Escape, or a click
│     away, [closes the box](leaveEdit) and keeps what you
│     wrote. The bar says unsaved until [ctrl-S keeps it in the
│     browser](save), so a box you come back to holds what you left.
│     Your words stay in the place you wrote them, even when the page
│     draws again between one box and the next. Only the box now open
│     answers a click away; an older box the page left behind closes
│     nothing.
│
●  you ask claude for an abstraction                  ([the menu](menuAt))
│     A right click opens a small menu where you point. On the header
│     of an abstraction it offers [a wider one above it](create) and
│     [to take that one away](deleteOpen); the ask to take away stands
│     on the head line itself, a click on its name [sends it](deleteSend),
│     and cancel, or escape, [lets it go](deleteClose). On
│     [words you picked](selectedRaw), in the text or in the open box,
│     it offers to expand on them: [a place opens on top of the
│     list](expandOpen) where you may add your own words, or none, a
│     click on its name [sends the ask](expandSend), and cancel
│     [drops it](expandClose). A file with no abstraction yet and some
│     code in it carries decompile over its writing place, which asks
│     for [the whole file to be read and told](decompile); an empty
│     file calls that place new abstraction, and a human file, which
│     has no code, calls it that too. Each of these [goes to the
│     server](ask) like a compile and comes back as a writing that
│     waits for claude.
│
●  you press compile and the server answers            ([compile](compile))
│     The button in the bar sends every place you changed, one after
│     the other, and each runs the command you would have typed. A
│     refusal comes back in the command's own words, named by the
│     place it came from, in the warning colour, and your words stay
│     on the page. A pass forgets the draft, redraws the page with
│     [the map read again](reloadMap) and says which writing now
│     waits for claude.
│
●  the page watches the queue                         ([pollQueue](pollQueue))
│     Every three seconds it asks the server what still waits and
│     marks the entries. When claude finishes, the mark goes, the
│     page reads the map of that file again, so the new words show,
│     and the training looks again for new rows.
│
●  you click                                                ([jump](jump))
│     A click on a header folds or unfolds that abstraction.
│     A click on a lit pin scrolls to the abstraction it points at,
│     unfolds it, and lights it for a moment; it opens no box.
│
●  you cross to another file                      ([crossJump](crossJump))
│     A pin can name a file of the project instead of a piece of
│     this one. A click on it opens that file and goes to the piece
│     the pin names. A pin to a file the project does not hold, or
│     to a piece with no abstraction, is muted and shows the piece
│     name. A pin can also name one abstraction of that file and
│     words inside it: a click opens the file, goes to that
│     abstraction, and lights those words for a moment. Such a pin
│     to words the abstraction does not hold is muted and shows the
│     file and the number of the abstraction; when the file holds no
│     such abstraction at all, a line on top says so.
│
●  the page shows the training                    ([loadTrain](loadTrain))
│     Every five seconds the page asks the server for the training
│     sessions. An open session covers the whole page with its rows.
│     Hide puts it away until the session gains a row, and [a short
│     line in the bar](chip) counts its rows and picks; a click on it
│     shows the training again. With no open session the line says
│     only training, and a click shows the last session. A list on
│     top goes to another session. When the store does not answer,
│     the line says why and takes no click. A session with no rows
│     yet says that claude writes them after the event.
│
●  you look through the rows                    ([renderRows](renderRows))
│     Each row is one change claude wrote for, and it fills the
│     screen; a swipe up brings the next row. A swipe to the side
│     goes to the next version of the same row: best, refinement and
│     free for a sync, best and free for any other. [A card](cardHtml)
│     names the file, the kind of change, the level and the entry, and
│     the version with its shape; a refinement that keeps the words
│     as they were is called current, and a row brought over from an
│     earlier session says carried. The words show with their pins,
│     but a pin here leads nowhere. When claude wrote a version more
│     than once, v1, v2 and on let you read each text; an older one
│     stands in a dashed frame, and the pick always takes the latest.
│     Copy [puts the words you see on the clipboard](copyText). A
│     version not written yet says so. A redraw keeps each row at the
│     version you had swiped to.
│
●  you pick a version                             ([sendPick](sendPick))
│     Pick this one opens a box for why you chose it, which you may
│     leave empty; pick sends it, and cancel drops it. The picked card
│     lights up and shows your why, and a press on it takes the pick
│     back. A refused pick says why in a line under the top bar. In a
│     finished session, or on a row already put in the map, a card
│     only says what was picked, or that it was taken by default, and
│     the entry it became.
│
●  you close the training                       ([closeTrain](closeTrain))
      Close training asks first and says [what the close will
      do](closeLine): how many rows are picked, how many take best,
      and how many carry over to the next session, a sync row with no
      pick and a row claude has not written yet. Close sends it;
      cancel, or escape, drops the ask. A pass reads the map of every
      file in the session again, puts the training away, and shows
      the server's answer on top of the reader. A refusal stays in the
      line under the top bar, and the session stays open.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  the look of the page                                    ([style](style))
     Two panes on a quiet ground: the tree on the left, the reader on
     the right, as wide as the window lets it. Text in a typewriter
     face, so drawings keep their columns. A dark and a light version,
     chosen by your system. On a narrow screen the tree hides and
     slides in over the reader. Over the files, new file and new human
     file wear the lively colour and underline themselves under the
     pointer, and the name box fills the rest of that line. The writing box sits in the place of
     the words, keeps the typewriter face, and grows with what you
     type. An empty place stands in its own room and lights up under
     the pointer, so you see where you can write. A word on a head
     line that does something wears the lively colour and underlines
     itself under the pointer. The little menu floats where you point,
     over everything, and each of its rows lights under the pointer.
     The training line in the bar wears the lively colour, and turns
     faint when the store does not answer. The training lies over the
     whole page: each row fills the screen and each card fills its
     width, and both snap into place, so one swipe moves one card. The
     name of a picked card wears the lively colour; an older text has
     a dashed frame. On a small phone the words of a card grow smaller.
